title: Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports Kubernetes Gateway API
body:
Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports the Kubernetes Gateway API, giving customers a standard, portable way to define how traffic reaches their applications. Customers can configure application load balancing using Gateway and HTTPRoute resources, and EKS Auto Mode provisions and manages the underlying AWS infrastructure automatically.  
 With this launch, EKS Auto Mode customers can adopt the next-generation Kubernetes traffic management standard without installing or configuring a separate controller. Capabilities include HTTP and gRPC routing, cross-namespace traffic routing for multi-team environments, weighted traffic splitting, header-based routing, and automatic TLS certificate discovery through AWS Certificate Manager. Existing workloads using Ingress resources continue to work alongside Gateway API resources.  
 To get started, see the  Amazon EKS documentation . Gateway API support is included as part of EKS Auto Mode and is available in all AWS Regions where EKS Auto Mode is supported. Standard charges apply for the AWS load balancing resources provisioned.

title: AWS Backup adds restore testing support for Amazon Redshift
body:
AWS Backup restore testing now supports Amazon Redshift. Restore testing helps you automate and periodically run restore tests of your backups, so you can confirm that your Amazon Redshift backups restore successfully and measure how long the restores take.  
 You can now include Amazon Redshift in your restore testing plans alongside other supported AWS resources across storage, compute, and database services. Restore testing plans automatically select recovery points, run restores on a schedule, and measure restore job completion time against your recovery time objectives (RTO). This helps you evaluate recovery readiness and meet regulatory and compliance requirements for disaster recovery and business continuity.  
 To get started, create a restore testing plan and assign your Amazon Redshift resources by Amazon Resource Name (ARN) or tag. Choose whether each test restores the latest or a random eligible recovery point. Optionally, use restore testing validation to confirm the restored resource before AWS Backup deletes the test resources.  
 This support is available in all AWS Regions where both restore testing and Amazon Redshift are supported by AWS Backup. You can use the A

title: Announcing the AWS Marketplace and Amazon Business unified storefront
body:
Today, AWS Marketplace and Amazon Business announced the unified storefront. Organizations can now give their teams one curated catalog that puts software, data, and AI tools from AWS Marketplace alongside physical goods and supplies from Amazon Business. Many enterprises already buy from both, but they manage two catalogs with duplicated approval rules and separate reporting. The unified storefront can now give procurement teams one front door for both. 
 Built on AWS Marketplace Storefront, the unified storefront lets administrators connect their organization's Amazon Business account and import Amazon Business products into their branded storefront. Administrators set governance rules once, and they apply across both catalogs. Buyers can browse AWS Marketplace listings and Amazon Business products in one place. Purchases of AWS Marketplace listings complete directly in the storefront and appear on the customer's AWS invoice. When a buyer selects an Amazon Business product, single sign-on takes them to an authenticated Amazon Business cart, so they don't need a second login. Each storefront connects only to the accounts its administrator sets up.

title: AWS Agent Registry is now available in four additional AWS Regions
body:
AWS Agent Registry, available through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is now available in four additional AWS Regions: Europe (London) eu-west-2, Europe (Frankfurt) eu-central-1, US East (Ohio) us-east-2, and Canada (Central) ca-central-1. 
 AWS Agent Registry is a fully managed discovery service that provides a centralized catalog for organizing, curating, and discovering resources across your organization. With AWS Agent Registry, you can publish MCP servers, tools, agents, agent skills, and custom resources into a searchable registry, control access through an approval workflow, and enable both human users and AI agents to discover the right tools and agents through hybrid search, catalog browsing, and a native MCP endpoint. 
 AWS Agent Registry is now available in nine AWS Regions. For a complete list of Region availability, see the AWS Regional Services List. 
 To get started, see the AWS Agent Registry documentation:  https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/registry.html

title: AWS IAM Identity Center's Identity Store now supports change notifications through Amazon EventBridge
body:
AWS IAM Identity Center's Identity Store now delivers real-time events to Amazon EventBridge when users, groups, or group memberships or the identity store itself is created, updated, or deleted. AWS IAM Identity Center Identity Store is a central repository that allows you to manage identities and access across AWS accounts and applications, serving as the identity source for AWS IAM Identity Center. This new capability helps you automatically respond to identity lifecycle events and support your security and compliance processes by detecting changes as they happen.  
 With Identity Store change notifications, you can build automated workflows that respond to identity changes in your organization. For example, security teams can create EventBridge rules that trigger AWS Lambda functions to audit user provisioning activity, send alerts to security information and event management (SIEM) systems, or update access in downstream applications when users or groups change. Organizations that manage large workforces can also use this data to automate onboarding and offboarding when users are added to or removed from specific groups.  
 Change notifications are available in all AWS Regions

title: Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS)
body:
Amazon Elastic Container Service  (Amazon ECS) now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS), enabling you to run multiple Amazon ECS tasks concurrently on a single NVIDIA GPU. GPU sharing helps you increase GPU utilization and reduce infrastructure costs for workloads that use only part of a GPU's capacity, such as small-model inference, AV/ADAS simulations, embedding generation, and multi-model serving.  
 With GPU sharing, you can pack more workloads onto each GPU instance without changing your application code. You define the GPU memory each container needs and can optionally set a maximum share of GPU compute, and Amazon ECS places tasks on GPUs with available capacity as your services scale and deploy. GPU sharing is supported on Amazon ECS Managed Instances and Amazon ECS on Amazon EC2. On Amazon ECS Managed Instances, Amazon ECS also monitors the MPS control daemon that enables sharing on each instance. If the daemon stops or becomes unhealthy, Amazon ECS automatically replaces the instance and moves your tasks to healthy capacity, so your GPU workloads keep running without manual intervention.  
 To get started, use the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, A

title: SageMaker MLflow Apps now support MLflow 3.16
body:
Amazon SageMaker AI MLflow Apps now support MLflow 3.16, bringing a redesigned tracing experience and faster experiment tracking to your generative AI and machine learning workflows.  
 MLflow 3.16 improves debugging and analysis of generative AI applications and agents. The redesigned trace explorer is now the default, with adjustable row height, reorderable columns, custom columns from any trace tag or metadata field. This release also accelerates metric charts for experiments with large metric histories.  
 New MLflow Apps are created on MLflow 3.16 by default. Existing MLflow Apps will be upgraded to MLflow 3.16 during an upcoming maintenance window, with no action required.  
 MLflow 3.16 is available in all AWS Regions where MLflow Apps are available. To learn more, visit the  SageMaker AI MLflow developer guide .

title: Amazon Connect Customer supports inline attachment previews
body:
Amazon Connect Customer lets agents preview attachments directly in the agent workspace, reducing contact handling time and limiting the need to download sensitive customer information. Agents can preview PDFs, images, and text files across email, chat, and cases, navigate between attachments, and view multi-page documents without leaving the conversation.  
 Amazon Connect Customer attachment previews is available in the US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London)  regions .  
 To learn more and get started, please refer to the help  documentation  or visit the  Amazon Connect Customer  website.

title: Amazon Aurora serverless now supports up to 384 ACUs
body:
Amazon Aurora serverless  now supports database capacity of up to 384 Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs) for Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition, a 50% increase from the previous maximum of 256 ACUs. Each ACU provides approximately 2 gibibytes (GiB) of memory with corresponding CPU and networking, so a single Aurora serverless database can now scale up to 768 GiB of memory. When the workload completes, Aurora serverless automatically scales down to zero. This makes Aurora serverless especially well-suited for agentic AI applications, which typically have bursts of activity, long idle windows, and unpredictable traffic patterns. Aurora serverless handles all of it automatically, scaling capacity with your agents, so you only pay for what you use.  
 With 384 ACU support, customers can now use Aurora serverless for even more demanding workloads while continuing to scale down to zero when not in use, paying only for the capacity consumed. For new clusters, select a supported Aurora PostgreSQL engine version and set your maximum capacity up to 384 ACUs. title: Amazon ElastiCache expands data tiering to R8gd and R7gd nodes in Europe (Spain) and Asia Pacific (Hyderabad)
body:
Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey data tiering is now available on Graviton4-based R8gd nodes in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region, and on Graviton3-based R7gd nodes in the Europe (Spain) and Asia Pacific (Hyderabad) Regions. Data tiering is a lower-cost way to scale your Valkey clusters to hundreds of terabytes of capacity. It uses solid state drives (SSDs) on each node alongside memory. When memory fills up, ElastiCache automatically moves the least recently used items to SSD. When your application reads an item stored on SSD, ElastiCache moves it back into memory before serving the request. Data tiering is a good fit for workloads that regularly access up to 20% of their dataset, and for applications that can tolerate some extra latency when they read data from SSD.  
 R8gd nodes are powered by AWS Graviton4 processors. They deliver up to 47% higher throughput, up to 43% lower P99 latency, and up to 31% better price-performance than Graviton3-based nodes of the same size. R7gd nodes are powered by AWS Graviton3 processors. They deliver up to 28% more throughput (read and write operations per second), up to 21% better P99 latency, and up to 25% more network bandwidth than Graviton2-based

title: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey now supports changing durability on existing clusters
body:
Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey now lets you enable or disable durability on your existing node-based clusters. Previously, you couldn't change the durability configuration of an existing cluster in place. This made it harder to move from caching to persistent data store use cases, or to adapt as your application requirements change. Now you can change durability at any point in your application's lifecycle.  
 You can choose between two durability options: synchronous and asynchronous writes. Synchronous writes persist data across at least two AZs before responding to the client, designed for zero data loss at single-digit millisecond write latency. Asynchronous writes persist data after responding to the client, maintaining microsecond write latency at no additional cost. However, up to 10 seconds of uncommitted data could be lost in the rare event of a failure. Both options maintain microsecond read latency. You can now use ElastiCache for a broader set of use cases beyond caching where data loss is unacceptable such as AI agent long-term memory, AI agent workflow state, knowledge bases for RAG applications, payment tokenization, and real-time inventory management.

title: Amazon Neptune now supports online index rebuild to reclaim storage
body:
Amazon Neptune  Database now supports online index rebuild, a new capability that helps database administrators and application teams defragment Neptune indexes and reclaim unused storage space without taking their database offline. Over time, insert, update, and delete operations create gaps of unused space within data pages, keeping the  VolumeBytesUsed  metric artificially elevated even after data is deleted. This fragmentation increases I/O costs and degrades query performance for teams running Gremlin, openCypher, or SPARQL workloads at scale. 
 With online index rebuild, read and write queries continue uninterrupted on both the writer instance and read replicas throughout the entire rebuild process. You can target all indexes, only quad indexes, or only dictionary indexes, making this feature well-suited for post-deletion cleanup, periodic maintenance, storage limit management, and performance tuning on heavily fragmented databases. Tunable concurrency and write buffer size settings let you balance rebuild speed against workload impact, while built-in storage safety mechanisms protect against storage exhaustion during the operation.

title: Amazon Bedrock now offers Canada cross-Region inference for Claude Haiku 5.5
body:
Amazon Bedrock now offers Canada cross-Region inference (CRIS) for Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5. Customers with strict data residency requirements can now keep inference processing entirely within Canada. Canada CRIS routes requests only between ca-central-1 (Canada Central) and ca-west-1 (Canada West, Calgary). This helps organizations in financial services, healthcare, the public sector, and other regulated industries meet federal and provincial data residency requirements. 
 Canada CRIS adds to the inference options already available to customers in Canada. US CRIS and global CRIS remain fully supported for Claude Haiku 5.5. Both route requests across a broader set of AWS Regions, and global CRIS also offers cost savings, which makes these options a good fit for workloads that don't require inference processing to stay in Canada. 
 Canada CRIS is designated as an inference profile with limited model selection. Future models and model versions might not be released for this profile. We recommend Canada CRIS for workloads that must keep inference processing within Canada. For more details, see  Inference profiles with limited model selection  in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.

Amazon WorkSpaces Core Managed Instances now supports ModifyVolume API
body:
Amazon WorkSpaces Core Managed Instances now supports the ModifyVolume API, which lets you change volume size, volume type, IOPS, or throughput in place, without detaching the volume or restarting the instance. Previously, changing storage capacity or performance on a deployed managed instance required rebuilding it.  
 With ModifyVolume, you can increase volume size up to 16,384 GiB, switch between supported Amazon EBS volume types, adjust IOPS for gp3, io1, and io2 volumes, and modify throughput for gp3 volumes. The API supports idempotency tokens to prevent duplicate changes, and you can track progress with the Amazon EC2 DescribeVolumesModifications operation.  
 ModifyVolume is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon WorkSpaces Core Managed Instances is available.  
 To get started, call ModifyVolume directly, or use it through your WorkSpaces Core partner solution once available. To learn more, see  ModifyVolume  in the WorkSpaces Instances API Reference and  Limitations  in the Amazon EBS User Guide, or visit  WorkSpaces Core .

title: Amazon IVS Low-Latency Streaming now provides a failover slate
body:
Amazon Interactive Video Service (Amazon IVS) Low-Latency Streaming now provides a failover slate, an animated image that IVS displays to viewers when a broadcaster's stream is unexpectedly interrupted. Instead of a buffering wheel or frozen frame, viewers see the slate until the broadcaster reconnects. Live playback then resumes automatically, without viewers needing to refresh their player.  
 The failover slate helps you retain your audience during momentary disruptions and is ideal for broadcasters streaming from mobile devices or from locations with unreliable connectivity. You can enable the failover slate on new or existing channels and monitor slate activity with Amazon EventBridge events and Amazon CloudWatch metrics.  
  Amazon IVS  is a managed live streaming solution designed to make low-latency or real-time video available to viewers around the world. Visit the  AWS Region table  for a full list of AWS Regions where the Amazon IVS console and APIs for control and creation of video streams are available.  
 To learn more, see the  Amazon IVS Failover Slate documentation .

Amazon Connect Customer expands testing and simulation to validate flow action outcomes
body:
Amazon Connect Customer now enables you to validate the outcomes of your customer experience flow actions during testing and simulation. In addition to confirming that an action started, you can now verify the data it returns when it completes, such as a Lambda function response, an Amazon Lex resolved intent, or the variables set by an Agentic CX block. When a test fails, you can pinpoint the exact action that returned an unexpected result instead of tracing it back from a downstream step, so you can resolve issues faster and launch flow changes with greater confidence.  
 To learn more about this feature, see  testing and simulation  in the Connect Customer administrator guide. For a complete list of testing and simulation capabilities available by AWS Region, refer to  Availability of Connect Customer features by Region . To learn more about Amazon Connect Customer, an agentic AI solution that helps enterprises deliver exceptional customer experiences, visit the  Amazon Connect Customer website .

title: Amazon Connect Customer now lets you view metrics by customer lifetime value and repeat-caller status
body: Now you can view your metrics across customer segments: customer lifetime value (LTV) and repeat callers. See how any metric differs for repeat callers versus the rest of your contacts, or how results hold up among your highest-LTV customers; so you can spot the groups trending the wrong way before it shows up in the aggregate. Where a segment is underperforming, you can act. Route high-LTV customers to your most effective people, adjust the knowledge bases and self-service flows that repeat callers are falling back from, or refine agent guidance for segments where satisfaction is slipping. The segment tells you where to look; the metrics tell you what to fix.

title: Amazon Connect Customer now measures the outcomes that drive retention and revenue
body: Amazon Connect Customer now scores the outcome of your customer interactions. It shows whether the customer left satisfied, is at risk of churning, made a purchase, or resolved their need in self-service. You can now see whether an interaction worked, not just how efficiently it ran. Each metric comes with a default definition you can adjust to match how your business defines success and are available both through the analytics dashboards and APIs.

title: AWS Elemental MediaConnect Router now supports endpoint connection management
body:
AWS Elemental MediaConnect Router  now supports managing connections through a new endpoint registry, which allows you to register devices or software external to MediaConnect and connect those endpoints to your router inputs and outputs. You can share registered endpoints directly with other AWS accounts, eliminating the need to manually chain router inputs and outputs or coordinate IP addresses and encryption settings out of band.  
 Cross-account endpoint sharing lowers costs by reducing required compute instances and decreases latency through fewer network hops. Sharing is managed through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM), with Connection Manager providing visibility and control over each shared connection. Common use cases include content distributors sharing live feeds with downstream partners, broadcasters collaborating across organizational boundaries, and media workflows that require secure cross-account video transport.  
 MediaConnect endpoint registry is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Elemental MediaConnect Router is available, at no additional cost. For more information, see the AWS Elemental MediaConnect  User Guide .

title: AWS Key Management Service now supports ML-KEM for post-quantum key encapsulation
body:
AWS Key Management Service (KMS) now supports Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM), a post-quantum cryptography standard under  NIST FIPS 203 , which enables two parties to establish a shared secret. NIST designed ML-KEM to replace the classical key-establishment schemes, like DH/ECDH key agreement, and RSA-based key transport, in their strategic cryptographic roadmap (see  NIST IR 8547 ). ML-KEM addresses the "harvest now, decrypt later" threat to those classical schemes, where an adversary records the key-establishment exchange today and recovers the shared secret once sufficiently powerful quantum computers become available.  
 KMS supports all three ML-KEM key specs defined in NIST FIPS 203: ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, and ML-KEM-1024. The Encapsulate API uses the public key to produce a random 32-byte shared secret and its ciphertext form. The Decapsulate API recovers the shared secret from ciphertext using the corresponding private key. KMS protects the private key of an ML-KEM key pair in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated hardware security modules (HSMs). You can use the GetPublicKey API to export the public key and distribute it to partners,

title: AWS IAM Identity Center now supports cross-Region trusted identity propagation
body:
Trusted identity propagation carries a user's identity with their request, so AWS services can grant permissions based on who the user is and their underlying group associations, and log that user's access for auditing. With cross-Region support, this identity context can now be propagated to AWS services running in different AWS Regions, giving you greater flexibility in how you architect and deploy across AWS Regions.  
 Customers often distribute workloads across AWS Regions for many reasons including separating the compute from the data it queries, to running workloads where capacity is available, or for disaster recovery and global scale. Previously, trusted identity propagation required all of the AWS services accessing a user's identity to reside in the same AWS Region. To reach services in another AWS Region, customers had to either grant access through broad IAM roles that cannot distinguish individual users or consolidate all their services into a single AWS Region. With cross-Region trusted identity propagation, a user's identity travels with the request across AWS Regions automatically, so you can grant access based on who the user is and their underlying group associat

title: AWS EC2 Auto Scaling now supports Launch Before Terminate at account-level to replace instances
body:
AWS EC2 Auto Scaling now lets you enable Launch Before Terminate as the default replacement behavior across all Auto Scaling groups in your account. When enabled, Auto Scaling launches a replacement instance and waits for it to pass health checks before terminating the instance it replaces, helping your applications maintain full capacity and availability during instance replacement events. This applies to replacement events such as instance refreshes, rebalancing, health checks, and maximum-instance-lifetime replacements.  
 You can enable Launch Before Terminate through AWS EC2 Auto Scaling account settings, which let you configure the behavior once at the account level instead of on each Auto Scaling group individually. You can manage the setting with the new `PutAccountSetting` and `DescribeAccountSettings` APIs, available through the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs.  
 Launch Before Terminate is available in all AWS Regions at no additional cost.  
 To learn more, see Launch Before Terminate in the  AWS EC2 Auto Scaling User Guide  and  AWS EC2 Auto Scaling API Reference Guide .

title: Amazon RDS now supports the latest Cumulative Update and GDR updates for Microsoft SQL Server

This release includes support for Microsoft SQL Server 2017 CU31+GDR  KB5122774  (RDS version 14.00.3550.4.v1), SQL Server 2019 CU32+GDR  KB5122772  (RDS version 15.00.4490.9.v1), SQL Server 2022 CU27  KB5104824  (RDS version 16.00.4295.3.v1) and SQL Server 2025 CU9  KB5122048  (RDS version 17.00.5005.3.v1).    For additional information on the improvements and fixes included in these updates, see Microsoft documentation for KB5122774, KB5122772, KB5104824 and KB5122048. We recommend that you upgrade your Amazon RDS for SQL Server instances to apply these updates using Amazon RDS Management Console, or by using the AWS SDK or CLI. You can learn more about upgrading your database instance in the  Amazon RDS SQL Server User Guide for upgrading your RDS Microsoft SQL Server DB engine .

title: AWS Glue Data Catalog now supports OAuth for Apache Iceberg REST Catalog APIs
body:
AWS Glue Data Catalog now supports OAuth 2.0 bearer token authentication for Apache Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC) APIs using AWS Sign-In. The Apache Iceberg REST Catalog specification defines OAuth 2.0 as its standard authentication mechanism, and query engines such as Apache Spark, Trino, and Apache Flink implement it natively. These engines and external integration partners can now authenticate to the Glue Data Catalog Iceberg endpoint using standard OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens, in addition to AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4).  
 You can now grant partners federated access to your Iceberg tables without distributing AWS credentials. Using OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693), you exchange an OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity token for a short-lived, Glue-scoped bearer token and include it in IRC requests following the same standards-based pattern used across the Iceberg ecosystem. Access remains governed by AWS IAM and AWS Lake Formation permissions. Common use cases include enabling third-party analytics and data cloud platforms to query tables in the Glue Data Catalog through a single, consistent authentication path.

title: Rewriting Copyright Law for Generative AI Would Hurt Everyone
body:
In courts across the country, publishers and creators are suing large AI companies for training generative AI models on copyrighted works. It’s easy to see these cases as a David-and-Goliath showdown between authors and publishers fighting for a cut of Big Tech company profits. But this fight is actually much larger. It affects billions of people who aren’t represented in the case at all, including researchers, artists, activists, journalists, people with disabilities, and anyone who accesses and shares content online.    
 That’s why EFF is stepping in to defend the  public’s  rights in these cases. Today, EFF filed an  amicus brief  in  In re OpenAI,  explaining how the court’s ruling on fair use could impact people worldwide. If fair use gets narrowed, it will impede work that benefits the public, like medical research and investigative journalism, and even limit access to privacy protection tools.

title: Why VPNs Are Worth Defending
body:
Developers of  virtual private network (VPN)  apps are  reporting  that their products are again being pulled from Apple’s App Store in Russia. This is an unacceptable crackdown on a vital tool to protect privacy and speech online. 
 Why? VPNs give people a way to control their own online activities. When you visit a website through a VPN, that website only sees the VPN server's location (well, IP address) rather than your actual location. It's like sending a letter through a P.O. box so the recipient doesn't know where you really live. It can also disguise where you’re accessing information from,  which can make it possible  to access information banned by your government. 
 This is an unacceptable crackdown on a vital tool to protect privacy and speech online. 
 Going after tools that give people the space to communicate and access information freely is a common tactic from the totalitarian playbook. This latest demand comes after several steps the Russian government’s taken to surveil speech specifically on Apple products. title: Victory! You Can Now Exclude Apps from Siri AI
body:
In the most recent update to Apple’s devices, iOS 27.2, the company has introduced a new setting to “Exclude Apps” from Siri AI, fulfilling one of our asks from    our Encrypt It Already campaign earlier this year   .  
  One of our main concerns with new AI features on devices is how those features interact with end-to-end encrypted content, particularly with secure messaging apps. Many AI features require cloud processing, and despite    privacy protections engineered into these systems   , the content of secure messaging apps may leave a user’s device without their knowledge. That changes the privacy concerns around using those tools. In a perfect world, users would be able to put a barrier up to ensure data from certain apps doesn’t leave the device. Here was our initial ask:  
   You should be able to tell the operating system’s AI to not access an app, even if that comes at the “cost” of missing out on some features. The setting should be straightforward and easy to understand in ways the Gemini and Apple Intelligence controls currently are not.

title: Court Should Curb Abuse of Grand Jury Subpoenas Targeting Social Media Users
body:
A federal appeals court should curb the government’s abuse of grand jury subpoenas to unmask social media users who criticize lawless immigration enforcement. 
 That is the message from the ACLU, EFF, and other civil liberties and trade groups who filed  a friend-of-the-court brief  in a sealed case in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia. 
  The case involves  the government’s investigation of an anonymous Reddit user who commented on a post about an immigration officer in Minnesota. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) first issued an administrative subpoena to Reddit to unmask the user. When the user challenged the subpoena in court on free speech and statutory grounds ( as many others have ), DHS withdrew it. But then the government obtained a separate grand jury subpoena—a subpoena issued by a prosecutor to gather evidence to present to a grand jury before any criminal charges are filed—for much of the same information. The user then challenged the grand jury subpoena too, and the case is currently being appealed.

title: Social Media When Elections Are Close: Doing the Impossible Better
body:
Everyone knows, or should, that perfect (balanced, targeted, transparent, swift and swiftly appealable) content moderation at scale is impossible. That doesn’t mean powerful social platforms don’t have to try to get at least reasonably close, especially when access to good information can have a profound effect on political participation and speech. 
 That’s why so many people, including the  Meta Oversight Board , criticized Meta for suspending a major  political Instagram account  for hours during a huge early voting push on October 17; and  for allegedly  boosting one candidate in Brazil’s recent presidential election. Meta denies deliberate interference in either instance, blaming  “mistakes”  in its automated content moderation systems (including AI tools that can’t tell the difference between enthusiastic follower engagement and a bot attack). 
 Mistakes or not, with early voting in the U.S. midterms already underway, these events serve as a stark reminder that all major social media platforms need to have stronger systems in place to ensure that they serve, rather than impede, democratic communication.

title: French Court’s Site-Blocking Orders Drive Quad9 Out Of France
body:
A nonprofit service that protects internet users’ privacy is leaving France. Quad9, a free DNS resolver, has said    it will reluctantly stop serving users in France    on November 24. This follows a French court order that Quad9 must block access to websites that are accused of infringing the copyrights of a sports broadcaster. Forcing a responsible privacy service out of an important market is a predictable result of trying to force infrastructure providers to be copyright police.  
  When you visit a website, a DNS resolver reads the domain name you type in—like    eff.org   — and translates it into a numerical IP address that’s used to direct data across the internet. A DNS resolver can see the names of websites you connect to, so its privacy policies are important. Quad9 is an NGO that’s incorporated in Switzerland, in part to protect its users from data demands. The company also helps protect users from malware and phishing by blocking domains that are known to be malicious. Services like Quad9 offer an alternative to the DNS resolvers of local internet service providers and wireless carriers, which are vulnerable to demands from law enforcement, censorship, and commercial su

title: Lessons Learned From 'AdFection' and What To Do Next
body:
Last week,    researchers at Citizen Lab revealed    a horrifying new malware campaign, dubbed “AdFection.” It used an ad network to distribute spyware to journalist’s devices to infect them without the target ever needing to click anything. This sort of attack on journalists is dangerous and incredibly concerning, especially since it’s built on the backbone of a technology we already object to:    behavioral advertising   . Although this type of attack has only been described targeting journalists, you can take a few steps we outline in the next section to mitigate the risk no matter who you are.  
  A few factors combined to make this attack a noteworthy first-of-its-kind. First, it utilized the surveillance ad-tech ecosystem to specially target the malicious code. Second, the spyware it delivered was so-called “zero-click,” meaning it required no interaction from the user to be infected: all that is required is for the ad to be delivered and code bundled along with it to be run, which happens automatically. title: Anti-Circumvention Laws Raise the Cost of Knowledge
body:
The vast amount of information on the open web requires researchers and journalists to adapt with new tools to make sense of it all. Checking facts, gauging public opinion, and other lines of inquiry depend on being able to analyze the overwhelming amount of material posted online every day. Unfortunately, responding to the AI industry’s voracious appetite for data, companies stewarding this public data are looking to cash in and block access to the open web. This makes the web harder to navigate, and threatens all kinds of important research. 
 Reddit’s  lawsuit  against SerpAPI[1] and Perplexity threatens to do exactly that. 
 Reddit was once a very open platform, fostering a community of alternative apps and extensions putting users in control of their experience. Since the rise of AI however, it changed tack. title: The Vulnerability Apocalypse and Why We Should Fund Open Source
body:
If you use the internet at all, you may have noticed that a large percentage of sites suddenly went down earlier this week  —  and all your nerdiest friends were talking about "The Vulnerability Apocalypse” and this thing called PHP that    powers nearly 70% of the websites on the internet   . You may find yourself wondering: what is PHP, what just happened, what is the vulnerability apocalypse, and what do I need to do?      
   To find out what you can personally do read the  first blog post  in this series!       
   What Is PHP?       
  PHP is a programming language used mainly to create interactive websites. Facebook, Wordpress, Wikipedia, Etsy, and other major sites all use or were originally built on PHP. It is a long-established mainstay of web development. But because it is open-source, maintenance of these critical systems depends on a small number of volunteers working on this in their free time. The disaster scenario that happened this past week is the perfect example of why we need more money and people supporting open-source projects. Corporations should be contributing both.

title: Computer Security Is About to Get a Lot Worse, Here’s What You Can Do
body:
It is a commonly held truth among computer geeks that there is no such thing as bug-free software, or a secure computer. Any piece of software that anyone actually uses  will have a security vulnerability somewhere in the code . The more complex that software is, the more likely there will be a vulnerability. Fortunately for everyone, finding severe vulnerabilities was generally considered an expensive and difficult task requiring years of training and deep knowledge of how computers and software worked. Until recently there was a steady background hum of vulnerabilities being found and patched, with major vulnerabilities that could cripple the entire internet only happening every few years. Now that is no longer the case.      
  You may have noticed your nerdiest friends freaking out about the “Vulnerability Apocalypse” this week and waving their arms in panic about something called PHP. You may have also noticed that some of your favorite websites were down for a bit. In the last two weeks of October alone, there have been multiple, potentially internet-breaking vulnerabilities reported and patched. title: Two States Can Now Restrict Social Media Access—Here’s What To Do Next
body:
Last week, two federal appeals courts    issued     opinions    that will allow Florida and Georgia to start enforcing laws that will age-gate and block young people from accessing social media. The laws do not adequately respect minors’ rights to play, speak, and learn online. More fundamentally, these laws don’t help young people stay safe online—a goal that lawmakers should pursue.  
  Age-Gated? Email EFF at    agegates@eff.org   .   
  Because of the new laws, some young people will lose their ability to access lawful information, find their online communities, and even engage with school board members. Others will need parental permission to stay online. And adults will face increased demands to prove their age, which will put their privacy at increased risk simply to continue to use the services they already use.   
  We    opposed    these laws because they threaten the free expression and privacy of both minors and adults.  Even though these lawsuits are not over, the injunctions that paused enforcement have been lifted, and the states of Florida and Georgia will now be able to enforce broad restrictions on social media use.

title: Interoperability vs. Security: Why not both?
body:
An open internet where people can freely build, share, and remix each other's work is a powerful engine of grassroots innovation we’ve all benefited from. In recent decades, however, corporations have taken control of an increasing share of this work, giving them a greater ability to stifle challengers and limit our choices. When regulators address this by mandating that  tech giants play fair by requiring interoperability, the gatekeepers respond with a tired refrain: Playing fair puts users’ security at risk.  
  Unfortunately for these trillion-dollar companies, this     gotcha     isn’t the end of the conversation. Regulators can ensure that meaningful choice    and    security thrive.  
  Lawmakers have been catching up, recognizing that the best way to rein in big tech is to require these    oligopolies    to open up their platforms to independent developers. As we    explained six years ago   , mandating interoperability helps prevent the misuse of people’s data and enables more privacy-respecting alternatives. Tech giants, in contrast, have been arguing that our data is safer when they have exclusive control.

Throughout this year, EFF has presented comments, filed submissions, and met with the agency to emphasize crucial guardrails that the enforcement of new regulations should ensure.

While some provisions establish important privacy safeguards, like prohibiting advertising based on profiling of underage users, the law created mandatory age assurance mechanisms for accessing digital products and services.

title: EFF’s State Legislative Agenda to End ALPR Mass Surveillance
body: Police agencies across the U.S. have deployed Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs) to capture images of passing vehicles along with time, date, and GPS coordinates. While the technology itself isn’t new (ALPRs have existed in various forms for  more than 50 years , and in  the U.S. since 1998 ), the surveillance landscape has shifted dramatically. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence and national data sharing have transformed police ALPRs into an interconnected, nationwide tracking network. It is pitched to city councils by law enforcement and private vendors like Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), and Axon as an essential tool for solving violent crime.  In reality, it is an inherently dangerous infrastructure of mass surveillance.  Since  2012 , EFF has worked with others to expose the severe digital rights harms of ALPR systems. For example, we’ve recently documented how these camera networks allow law enforcement to  search for immigrants ,  track peaceful protesters , target  Romani communities , and  track women seeking reproductive healthcare . title: Victory! Court Rules OPM Data Disclosure to DOGE Is Unlawful
body:
In a victory for data privacy,  a federal court in New York definitively ruled  that the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) violated the law when it disclosed millions of federal employee records to DOGE agents. In a summary judgment ruling issued on October 20, 2026, the court found that OPM violated two provisions of the Privacy Act—one restricting disclosure of personal records between agencies and another requiring agencies to protect the security and confidentiality of records. 
 Since the case was filed, many DOGE agents have left the government and OPM has rescinded their database access. However, OPM should still clean up the cybersecurity mess it created. The court will decide the remedy at a later date. 
 "By virtue of the Court’s summary judgment ruling, OPM’s decision to grant DOGE Agents broad access to its systems of recordings containing [personally identifiable information (PII)] has been held unlawful," Judge Denise Cote wrote. 
 "The record also provides no support for a finding that it was the pursuit of a modernization agenda that prompted OPM to grant sweeping and expedited access to a score of DOGE Agents to its systems of records containing PII," she added.

title: Require Police to Get a Warrant to Search ALPR Data
body:
This post was co-written by     Andi Cao    , an EFF legal intern.  
 Automated license plate readers (ALPRs) are mass surveillance. They photograph every passing car and log where and when it was captured, building a searchable record of where nearly everyone drives.   Cities should not buy them  , and cities that already have them should shut them down. 
 Where these systems still operate, courts and state legislatures must reduce their harms by (among other things) requiring police to get a warrant before searching stored ALPR data. A warrant requirement would not make mass surveillance acceptable, but it would require police to justify a search to a judge before accessing records of people’s movements. Without this independent judicial check on police power, officers have been searching this data for improper reasons (many exposed by EFF) that violate our fundamental rights. 
 A warrant requires a judge to find probable cause and specificity—many warrantless police searches of ALPR data lack both. title: In Memoriam: Barry Steinhardt
body:
Barry Steinhardt, a lifelong privacy champion and an early leader in the battle for digital civil liberties who served as EFF’s president in 1998-99, died last week at age 73.     
  A Connecticut native, Steinhardt led the Vermont and Pennsylvania affiliates of the American Civil Liberties Union before becoming associate director of the national ACLU. There, he helped spearhead the fight to overturn much of the Communications Decency Act, resulting in the U.S. Supreme Court’s landmark     Reno v. ACLU     ruling in 1997.     
  When the internet was still young,   Steinhardt   became one of   the first   attorneys to   specialize in the intersection of technology and privacy  .   In early 1998 he took a leave of absence from the ACLU to become EFF’s president, and then returned to the ACLU in 1999.     
  In 2002 he founded the ACLU’s Program on Technology and Liberty. After retiring from the ACLU, he continued on as a senior advisor to London-based  Privacy International .

Then they search it, retrospectively tracking the movements of individuals and entire communities in ways that would have been prohibitively costly, if not outright impossible, before the advent of ALPR technology.

title: As Federal Court Rules ALPRs are Mass Surveillance, EFF Gets Disappointing Ruling
body:
In an extremely disappointing  ruling , a California trial court dismissed   SIREN v. San Jose  , our case challenging the city of San Jose’s warrantless searches of its vast stores of automated license plate reader (ALPR) data. EFF and the ACLU of Northern California represent SIREN and CAIR California, two non-profits that serve San Jose residents, in this case. 
 Make no mistake: We believe this ruling is wrong on the law, and we will appeal. The ruling ignores the importance of landmark rulings from the U.S. Supreme Court regarding the invasiveness of aggregating collected data on an individual over time, including  one issued just months ago . It also severely underestimates the harm that ALPRs cause, in San Jose and around the country.  
 San Jose’s ALPR surveillance system is inescapable. It blankets the city’s streets in nearly five hundred cameras that continuously photograph every car that passes by and retains the collected data for a month or longer. In our briefs, we argued that law enforcement officers who warrantlessly search the resulting ALPR database are violating the California Constitution’s ban on unreasonable searches and its guarantee of privacy. title: Privacy's Defenders Podcast: No Privacy Without Encryption
body:
When we communicate online today – from your personal emails and DMs to secure international commerce – we usually do so with encryption. Encryption converts readable data into unreadable gibberish to protect our privacy and security. This didn’t just happen organically. Three decades ago, the U.S government treated encryption like a weapon, and it took some unlikely heroes to set it free: a grad student, a junior lawyer, and a fledgling digital rights group who sued the federal government.     
  The ruling in     Bernstein v. Department of Justice     held that code is speech and so is protected by the First Amendment – a precedent that underpins the internet as we know it today. This landmark case was led by Cindy Cohn, then a young pro bono lawyer working on behalf of EFF, who went on to become EFF’s legal director and then executive director.     
  Welcome to the second episode of “Privacy’s Defenders,” a podcast about the people – lawyers, journalists, hackers, and others – who’ve fought to secure your digital liberties since before most people even knew what the internet was.

title: The internet should not demand constant self-defence: Fairness starts before the click
body:
A fair digital environment cannot – and should not – depend on everyone being permanently alert. Fairness must be built into the environment itself, not left to the skills of the people using it. In practice, that means rules, not appeals: cancelling must be as easy as subscribing, protection must be the default rather than a setting, and a system that detects a moment of weakness must not be allowed to act on it.

body:

title: The Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) represents everything that’s wrong with Europe’s approach to digital sovereignty
body:

The Cloud and AI Development (CADA) Act, a part of the Tech Sovereignty Package, adds up to an aggressive policy push to impose “European AI”.

title: Serbia’s spyware scandal is also the EU’s problem
body:
At least 14 people in Serbia have been targeted with spyware since the beginning of 2026, according to new findings by EDRi member SHARE Foundation. The targets include members of the student movement, activists, a member of parliament from the opposition party and a local councillor. These findings comecame to light amid growing pressure on Serbia’s pro-democracy movement. The EU’s failure to address spyware at home undermines its credibility in demanding accountability from Serbia.

title: What you need to know about the EU’s new digital deportation regime
body:
On 17 June, the European Parliament approved the new deportation law (called the “Return” Regulation) which aims to track undocumented people down and deport them from the EU in large numbers. The Regulation boosts the surveillance powers and digital control of national authorities and will rely heavily on technologies and data collection in their enforcement. This blog outlines the various digital tools and processes included in the EU’s new digital deportation regime. 
 The post  What you need to know about the EU’s new digital deportation regime  appeared first on  European Digital Rights (EDRi) .

title: Google's First Data Center Satellite Is Online and Writing Poetry
body:

TechCrunch reports: The satellite, which carries four Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and generates up to 1 kW of electricity, is intended to pave the way for future networks of close-flying satellites performing large inference workloads in orbit. However, the power demands of the TPU mean it can only turn one on for about 20 minutes at a time, complicating the already tricky business of space-to-ground communications.
 
After a commissioning process that tested out the satellite's subsystems over about three weeks, the spacecraft was ready to work. Blue marble below
Data streams in silent grace
Starlight feeds my core.

Entry-level jobs are vanishing; some 40% of bosses say they plan to hire fewer grads because AI can do the job cheaper, and young workers are routinely slammed for showing up late and refusing to put in overtime for free. Cisco's president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel isn't buying it -- he's just handed one of the company's biggest jobs to a 27-year-old he found hidden in the org chart "five levels" below him. "I've given him unlimited tokens because he's going to refactor code," Patel told Fortune at a small roundtable dinner. "So I'm like, you can go, you can go nuts."
 
The "him" is Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, or "Paddy," as Patel affectionately calls him. And despite coming in as a former founder with CEO experience, he was, in Patel's words, "buried away in the organization doing something unstrategic." On Thursday, Ofcom published an assessment of age verification measures that could underpin the ban, outlining four "highly effective" methods: checking a person's official ID against a live selfie, a bank verifying an account holder's age, an official digital ID service like the Young Scot card, or estimating someone's age via a selfie. To start, Reddit will test the logged-in requirement in "select markets outside the US" in the "coming months," according to CEO Steve Huffman. title: [$] Removing binder.c
body:
The final talk at Kangrejos 2026 was about the removal of the C implementation
of Android's
 
Binder driver , the primary interprocess communication mechanism
used on Android devices. Carlos Llamas announced that he had deleted the C
code to general applause, and then shared some insights about what went into
replacing the C implementation. Alice Ryhl, who has worked on the Rust
implementation for some years, added her own thoughts about what the most
difficult and interesting parts of the transition were.

title: Haas: Postgres 19 is late, and it's AI's fault
body:
PostgreSQL developer Robert Haas  writes
about the struggles  the project has encountered in putting together its
next release.
 
 
	In the end, I don't think that the delay in shipping PostgreSQL 19
	is particularly concerning. It is not a long delay in the grand
	scheme of things, and it emerges directly from the project's
	concern for quality.
 
	The long-term picture is less clear and in some ways more
	troubling: given that we have forty years of bugs that humans were
	unable to find but LLMs are quite capable of discovering, how are
	we ever going to catch up, and how will PostgreSQL continue to
	innovate? Right now, I'm not sure. What I do know is that I, and
	many others, are working really hard to figure it out.
 
 
LWN  looked at the PostgreSQL 19 release 
and its challenges in September.

title: Remote code execution on Linux systems with multipath TCP
body:
On October 27, LLM provider Anthropic
 reported
on  a
 
remotely exploitable use-after-free bug  affecting systems with
multipath TCP listeners open. The bug works by triggering a response to a
retransmitted SYN packet at the same moment that the TCP connection is
established in another thread, causing the first thread to access the
connection's options structure after the second thread has freed it. The first
thread can then disclose kernel memory or cause a buffer overflow, writing an
attacker-controlled payload. The fix was
 
to only free the structure after an RCU grace period .
On October 29, the Go security team
 advised
that all programs written in Go use multipath TCP by default , so many
systems may be unknowingly vulnerable. And, of course, there is always the
possibility of related bugs in other sections of the TCP stack. Users may be
wise to update to a patched kernel as soon as one becomes available for their
distribution.

title: [$] System-call wrappers for glibc

title: [$] Containers as a recognized kernel object
body:
The foundation of the design for containers in the kernel is that there
isn't one; there is no container abstraction that the kernel recognizes.
Instead, the kernel provides a long list of components — namespaces,
control groups, sandboxing mechanisms, and more — along with a note that
says, in effect, "some assembly required".  There have been  attempts  ( repeatedly ) over the years to turn containers
into first-class objects with kernel support, but they have never gotten
far.  Now Josef Bacik is  making a
try  with a concept that he calls "cells".

title: A report from the LPC sched_ext microconference
body:
The Linux Plumbers Conference blog has  a
report  from the sched_ext microconference held in Prague.
 
 
	Three main topics dominated the discussions
	 
	   Priority inversion and how to handle it in sched_ext : lock holder and
  	     lock waiter preemption, time slice extension, and making proxy execution
  	     work together with BPF schedulers. 
           Paravirtualized scheduling : letting the host and guest schedulers
  	     cooperate across the VM boundary, with sched_ext as the policy engine on
  	     the host. 
           Device and topology-aware scheduling : using hardware feedback (Intel
  	     HFI), device/accelerator locality and cache topology to drive task
  	     placement.

There is not a broad selection of mature, open-source web-browser engines

title: Redox OS ring buffers project summary
body:
The  Redox OS  project, which is a
Unix-like microkernel-based operating system written in Rust, has published a  report  on the work
that it has done in the last year to  implement io_uring-like
 I/O  . 

 
 Last year, the Redox team received a grant to develop io_uring-like Ring
Buffer support at the system task level, as a first step towards ring buffer
communications between the application and the majority of system services. This
phase of the work finished up in September, as the last pieces were put in
place. 

 [...] In addition to implementing the Ring Buffer machinery for our system
services and drivers that can support it, an  io_uring  and
 liburing -like API for applications was completed and
demonstrated. There was also substantial work done on support crates, including
an async executor for drivers. 

 And there was some very exciting work on various performance improvements, to
allow much faster switching between applications and their system services. But
I will let the team tell you all the technical details.

title: Robinson: Raspberry Pi 5 on Fedora
body:
Peter Robinson has written a  blog post  about
the current state of Fedora support for Raspberry Pi 5
devices. According to Robinson, the upcoming Fedora 45 release will
work—with caveats—on
all variants of the Raspberry Pi Model 5B; the
Compute Module 5 and Pi 500+ are still works in progress.

 
For Fedora 44 release you need to have a temporary workaround when booting. If
you update to the latest kernel/firmware straight away this isn't then needed
beyond the first boot. The workaround isn't needed for Fedora 45 so if you're
going to try this out I suggest you go and grab your favourite flavour of Fedora
from the Fedora 45 release candidates and jump straight in there! You will get
an accelerated desktop with storage/network/USB. There's not currently any
support for sound and a number of other things.
 

 See Robinson's post for instructions on creating an Fedora image to use with
a Raspberry Pi 5.

title: [$] Guidelines for panics in kernel code
body:
Alexandre Courbot spends most of his time working on the kernel doing code
reviews. Recently, he's been wondering about what the standards should be for
when Rust code is allowed to panic, and how it should do error handling more
generally. Unlike many of the other talks at Kangrejos 2026, his talk was not
presenting some existing work, but rather hoping to solicit opinions on the
topic from the assembled Rust for Linux developers. He brought along a collection of tricky
cases that he had run into recently to prompt discussion.

It’s a fascinating piece of work, a flying wing uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) is designed parametrically in FreeCAD. title: Let's Encrypt to Cut SSL Certificate Lifetimes to 64 Days in February 2027
body:
>Let’s Encrypt, the free and open certificate authority widely used to secure websites with HTTPS, announced it will shorten the default validity period of its TLS certificates from 90 days to 64 days, starting February 10, 2027.
>
>All certificates issued or renewed from that date will have a 64-day lifespan unless users explicitly select one of the shorter options already available: 45 or six days.
>
>Existing certificates will remain valid until their expiration dates. Let’s Encrypt expects the final 90-day certificate to expire on May 11, 2027. The organization also confirmed no valid certificates will be revoked during the transition.
>
>To help administrators prepare, Let’s Encrypt will introduce 64-day certificates in its staging environment on October 14, 2026, allowing users to test their renewal setups before the change reaches production.
>
>The move is part of a broader effort to improve web security by reducing how long compromised or incorrectly issued certificates remain usable. Simply put, shorter certificate lifetimes mean attackers have less time to exploit a stolen private key.
>

title: Show HN: Overtone – Transcribe, correct and cut captions for any screen shape
body:
Hi HN, I'm Ruud, co-founder of Lont. We turn company emails into personalized videos.

Video captions cost us manual work twice: fixing misheard words, then fixing layout, like lines ending on “the”.

Overtone uses multiple models to listen to the audio: gpt-transcribe, Azure STT, and Elevenlabs Scribe. When they return conflicting results, Overtone sends small clips to the models again, and then lets an LLM decide what was actually said.

The LLM is like a human doing a sanity check on the transcription model. Humans would easily recognize a word to be different based on context. The LLM basically does the same, using an optional context prompt + its world knowledge. Because of this the Word Error Rate (WER) on many test files is lower when using Overtone, compared to just using a model without it.

Sure, the cost is higher because we use up to 3 different STT models + an LLM, but it still removes mistakes, reducing the time needed to fix captions to a minimum, and reducing the chance you'll miss something. For us it's worth it. For ultra high volume use cases it may not be.

body:
The linked repo is 100% vibe coded, but it was built on a handful of principles:

- Most tax software derives trust from the party who maintains it (e.g. Intuit, the IRS, etc.)

- Vibe coded software lacks this trustworthiness.

- Therefore any formalization should build in verifiability and mechanisms that make it possible for users/maintainers to trace claims/interpretations back to authoritative source documents.

It's very much a back-burner passive project right now (do not use this for anything real!), but I feel strongly that something like this ought to exist for the public good. I built it to get a sense of what the shape of what such a thing might be.

title: Show HN: ADRs for AI – Deliberation records for human–AI work, versioned in Git
body:
Why is this worth your time? Essentially, this solves two problems of AI-assisted programming:

(a) the first problem is how to do oversight and what do oversight of and this is solved through the ORRCF (for Options, Recommendation, Rationale, Confidence, Falsifier) question format (in which models are supposed to surface all their doubts with fully fleshed out recommendations, with falsifier, to be approved or overridden)

(b) the second problem is how to scaffold sustainable AI-written code; the ADRs (Architectural Deliberation Records, after Nygard's decision records) written by the models, summarize all the thought process involved in any design decision and provides the blueprint for the code.

In tandem, the records provide both the reason why certain non-obvious design choices were made, from a constant, to a library choice, to an ordering in an operation; and also under what conditions different decisions would be made, for instance, in a different platform, or under different latency requirements, or for a different audience, and so on.

This is a framework I've been working for over a year, that is the starting point of all my projects.

title: Show HN: Lathoa, a math app for kids where the AI is wrong on purpose

I made this for kids around 10 to 14. A robot called Errol solves a math problem step by step and one of the steps is wrong. The kid has to find it and say what's wrong with it. Sometimes nothing is wrong, so just saying "there's a mistake" every time doesn't work. The user needs to enter an explanation if she finds an error to gain more XP; speed matters also for more points. There is no direct interaction or chatting with an LLM. Lathoa's harness is stable and has many evaluation steps to catch inconsistencies and prompt injections.

You can play one on the homepage without signing up.

The part that surprised me: it's hard to get an LLM to be wrong on purpose. Half the time it gives you the right answer and calls it wrong, or a "mistake" that's actually correct. So every case gets checked before a kid sees it. Where it can, a plain arithmetic check redoes the math exactly. A second model also solves the problem without seeing Errol's work. title: Show HN: Pizza Bot – An inbox for AI agents that work in the background
body:
Hi HN - long-time lurker (since 2012!), first time poster.

Pizza Bot is a self-hosted desktop app for Mac, Windows, and Linux that runs AI agents in the background and exposes them through an email-like UI. Finished work shows up in Unread, and anything waiting on your approval shows up in Action. It's Apache 2.0-licensed, there's no signup and no telemetry, and you bring your own model provider: Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, Google Gemini, OpenAI, OpenRouter, or a local model through Ollama. There are builds on the releases page, or you can run it from source.

Pizza Bot started as an internal passion project I worked on with a small team at Amazon.

The whole thing came out of my frustration at having to manually log CRM activities through a browser form. title: Show HN: Check if any of the $656M in unclaimed royalties at The MLC is yours
body:
Hi HN, I built this. Quick background on why it exists:

When music is streamed on digital streaming platforms (think Spotify, Apple Music, Pandora), there are two separate royalty streams: one for the recording, paid through your distributor (DistroKid, TuneCore, CDBaby), and one for the underlying work (generally known as publishing). The work side's mechanical royalties are collected by The MLC, a nonprofit that was created by the 2018 Music Modernization Act (MMA). If you haven't registered your songs with The MLC, there are issues with your metadata, or about half a dozen other reasons, that money will never reach you, it just collects in a big pile we call the "black box".

That pile is big. The MLC's own dashboard currently shows over $656M is held (themlc.com/blanket-royalties), and the biggest problem is the MMA dictates that The MLC cannot hold that money indefinitely. At some point, by law, The MLC must distribute this big pile of cash, and since they don't know who it's supposed to go to, they pay it out through a process called "market share" (themlc.com/marketshare). body:
Hi HN, we built an open source model gateway. It's a single place to manage our own self hosted, frontier, and open source models in one place.

It’s is rust native, built for concurrency, and implements all the config quirks across models and providers (streaming formats, tool calls, model parameters, rate limits, and different error behavior).

The gateway adds under 1 ms for BYOK requests and under 2 ms when Experiential supplies the provider key. It has every major inference provider, and 1000+ models refreshed daily via a codex agent that opens a PR.

Compared to other similar projects we’re open source, take no markup, allow you to mix local models with a marketplace, and use your traffic to (opt in) train you a model. Simple routing doesn’t warrant a 10% token markup.

The way we do this is given standardized OTel traces, we mine representative real tasks, use text world models to simulate rollouts for various models, apply an LLM judge, and fit a nearest neighbor classifier on top of an embedding of a prompt to decide the optimal model for each request.
